records.name_note: Sources split on which common name leads. NC State's page title reads 'Magnolia acuminata (Cucumber Magnolia, Cucumber Tree, Cucumber-tree, Cucumbertree Magnolia)' and its Common Name(s) field stacks the same four entries in the same alphabetized order, so NC State's lead entry is 'Cucumber Magnolia'; its Description prose, however, calls the species 'Cucumber Tree.' MoBot's Common Name field displays a single value, 'cucumber tree.' RHS's H1 is the botanical name alone, with 'cucumber tree' as the plant-profile subtitle and page-title name, and 'blue magnolia' listed separately under Other common names. 'Cucumber-tree' and 'Cucumbertree Magnolia' appear only as later entries in NC State's list. Two of the three dedicated pages lead with cucumber tree, so Cucumber Tree is used here.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail left null: NC State's page (which does carry a structured Poison block on species where one exists) shows no Poison Part/Severity/Symptoms information for this species, and neither MoBot nor RHS mentions toxicity to cats, dogs, or any other animal for Magnolia acuminata.

day_f_min/max, night_f_min/max, humidity_need, humidity_pct_min/max, light_fc_min, light_fc_good, chill_damage_f, and cool_rest_note left null: no admissible source states an onset temperature, a day/night range, a humidity percentage or need tier, or a foot-candle light figure for this outdoor canopy tree. RHS's cultivation note that 'late frost may damage the flower buds' is a frost-risk mention, not a stated onset temperature, so chill_damage_f was left null per the rule against deriving onset figures from non-numeric hedges.

direct_sun_hours_max left null: NC State's Light field gives hour ranges (6+ hours for Full sun; 2-6 hours for Partial Shade), but these are the site-wide category legend text tied to the Light field's category names, not species-specific prose, so they were not used to set an hour figure.

outdoor_sun_exposure = [full_sun, part_shade]: NC State's Light field (Full sun; Partial Shade), MoBot's Sun field (Full sun to part shade), and RHS's Position field (Full sun, Partial shade) all agree exactly, so no single-source shade tag needed to be excluded here.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State's Soil pH field lists only an open-ended 'Acid (<6.0)' band and a closed 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)' band, but RHS's pH field lists 'Acid or Neutral or Alkaline,' accepting soils on both sides of Neutral. Per the cross-check rule, RHS accepting alkaline rules out a ceiling and RHS accepting acid rules out a floor, so both were left null. NC State's own Description prose also says the species 'tolerates a wide range of pH.'

water_regime and the water day-interval/dry-down fields left null: MoBot's only structured moisture cue is 'Water: Medium,' a mid-scale rating that cannot support keep_moist per the rules, and no admissible source frames watering for this species in dry-down, keep-moist, or day-interval terms; NC State's 'prefers moist well-drained soil...sensitive to heat and drought' is a soil/tolerance statement, not a watering-frequency instruction. As an in-ground canopy tree, the day-interval and dry-down-target fields were left null per the rule for in-ground trees/shrubs/perennials.

fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, and fertilize_strength left null: none of the admissible sources give a fertilizing schedule or dilution strength for this species, and no genus-level commercial-crop source was used per the rule against borrowing production schedules.

An earlier automated extraction pass returned a purported NC State 'is often confused with' module naming Magnolia ashei and Magnolia macrophylla; a direct render of the live NC State page showed no such module present, so that claim was discarded rather than cited to avoid reporting fabricated content.

records.toxicity_detail: NC State's structured Poison block (human-scoped) gives Poison Severity "Medium"; Poison Symptoms: "Poisonous if ingested especially the nuts. Symptoms may include muscle weakness and paralysis, dilated pupils, vomiting, diarrhea, depression, paralysis, and stupor."; Poison Toxic Principle: "Glycose aesculin, saponin aescin, possibly alkaloids."; and the full Poison Part list: "Bark, Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Seeds, Stems". Causes Contact Dermatitis: "No". NC State's Plant Type field co-lists the trait "Poisonous" (Perennial, Poisonous, Shrub, Woody Plant). Separately, NC State's Problems tags carry "Poisonous to Humans," "Problem for Cats," "Problem for Dogs," and "Problem for Horses" -- the Cats/Dogs tags are the basis for toxic_to_pets=true, distinct from the human-scoped Poison Severity rating. UF/IFAS (ask.ifas.ufl.edu, FP017) separately states: (a structured Toxicity field value, rendered in lower case with no terminal period) "all parts of this plant exhibit medium toxicity if ingested; poison toxic principles include glycose aesculin, saponin aescin, and alkaloids", and warns "Care should be used with this plant around pets and children, as all parts of the plant are toxic if ingested, especially the nuts produced in the fall" -- this UF/IFAS pet mention is unscoped as to which pet species, so it corroborates but does not independently establish the cats/dogs scoping. Clemson's dedicated grow-and-care page adds a handling warning: "Don't be tempted to eat the seed as they are poisonous to people and pets." RHS's Potentially harmful field states "Humans/Pets (dogs): harmful if eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling", adding a dog-scoped hazard statement and a protective-equipment handling instruction. No source disagreement on edibility exists: NC State ("Flowers are followed by the nut called a buckeye and are not edible"), MoBot and Clemson all agree the seed is not edible.
records.water_estimate_basis: Clemson HGIC's dedicated grow-and-care page states watering as a weekly cadence in its Quick Guide: 'Deeply once a week; more often in hot, dry spells.' It is the only cited source giving a literal interval, so water_growing_days_est is 7 (weekly restated in days); no dormant-season interval is stated, so water_dormant_days_est is null. This is general in-ground care guidance, not a measured soil dry-down schedule.
unknowns: No admissible source gives a numeric soil pH ceiling or floor: NC State's Soil pH field reads only the open-ended "Acid (<6.0)" band, and the RHS species details page for Aesculus parviflora (589) carries a Soil Types field (Chalk, Clay, Loam, Sand) but no numeric pH field, so soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are left null.

water_regime is left null: the only literal watering statement (Clemson, "Deeply once a week; more often in hot, dry spells") does not map cleanly onto keep_moist/keep_barely_moist/dry_surface_between/dry_thoroughly_between, and MoBot's structured Water field reads only "Medium" (mid-scale), which per the rules is a disclosed counterpoint, not a basis for keep_moist.

outdoor_sun_exposure excludes full_sun even though RHS's Position field lists "Full shade, Full sun, Partial shade": both North American structured sun fields (NC State Light Conditions: Dappled Sunlight, Deep shade, Partial Shade; MoBot Sun: "Part shade to full shade") exclude full sun, and UF/IFAS (ask.ifas.ufl.edu FP017) states the plant "thrives in partial to full shade," so RHS's UK-calibrated full-sun listing is treated as excluded/disclosed rather than carried.

soil_drainage is set to moderate based on NC State's own structured Soil Drainage field ("Good Drainage, Moist, Occasionally Wet"), per the rule that this field must be read first. UF/IFAS separately lists an "Extended flooding" tolerance and NC State's own field includes "Occasionally Wet" -- both are disclosed as counterpoints/tolerance traits, not used to push the value to moisture_retentive.

No admissible source gives foot-candle light figures, a species-specific direct-sun-hour maximum, temperature ranges (day/night), humidity percentage or need, chill-damage onset temperature, or any fertilizing schedule/strength for this species specifically, so those fields are left null. A Penn State, UMD, or Georgia CAES page specific to this species was not found in this research pass.

RHS's page also lists 'Other common names: dwarf buckeye, dwarf horse chestnut' -- a secondary field, not treated as a competing lead name since NC State, MoBot, Clemson, and UF/IFAS/ask.ifas.ufl.edu all independently use 'bottlebrush buckeye' as the working common name.

records.name_note: Sources split on which name leads. NC State's Common Name(s) field is a two-entry stacked list, "Franklinia" then "Franklin Tree", and its page title parenthetical carries the same two names in the same order: "Franklinia alatamaha (Franklinia, Franklin Tree)". By contrast, both RHS and MoBot are dedicated single-species pages that carry a single common name value: RHS's page title/subtitle reads "Franklinia alatamaha | Franklin tree" and MoBot's Common Name field reads "Common Name: Franklin tree" with no second name listed and no Common Names tooltip present on the page. Because two of the three admissible sources with dedicated single-species pages lead with "Franklin tree" alone, that name is used as common_name here, with "Franklinia" noted as NC State's co-listed alternate.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets/toxicity_detail left null: none of the admissible sources (NC State, MoBot, RHS) carry a Poison/toxicity field or any toxicity statement for this species. NC State's page has no Poison field or Poisonous Plant Type/Problems tags at all.

soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max left null: NC State's Soil pH field selects only "Acid (<6.0)", which is open-ended downward and so gives no floor. Its 6.0 top is not usable as a ceiling either, because RHS's pH field reads "Acid or Neutral", extending above 6.0 with no numeric bounds given. With the two admissible sources disagreeing on the top of the range and neither giving a floor, both bounds are left null.

water_regime left null: no admissible source gives a watering-cadence statement (dry-between, keep-moist, etc.) for this species. MoBot's structured Water field reads "Water: Medium", which per the rubric is mid-scale and cannot support keep_moist; it is a disclosed counterpoint only, not a basis for any enum value.

water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing/dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis left null: this is an in-ground landscape tree/shrub and no source frames watering with a dry-down depth or day-interval cadence.

day_f_min/max, night_f_min/max, humidity_need, humidity_pct_min/max, light_fc_min/good, chill_damage_f, cool_rest_note, fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, fertilize_strength all left null: no admissible source frames care for this hardy outdoor tree in these houseplant-style terms (indoor temperature ranges, foot-candles, humidity percentage, fertilizer dilution/schedule). NC State's USDA Plant Hardiness Zone list (5a-8b) is a survival-zone range, not a damage-onset temperature, so it cannot support chill_damage_f per the rubric.

direct_sun_hours_max left null: NC State's Light entries read "Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)" and "Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)". Those hour figures are NC State's site-wide light-category legend definitions, not species-specific prose for Franklinia alatamaha, so they are excluded per the rubric.

Root-disturbance, transplant-difficulty, and heat warnings (decision-relevant but no matching schema field): NC State: "It can be difficult to transplant because of a sparsely fibrous root system, so plan well when choosing its planting location." and "In general, this tree has a reputation for being difficult to grow." and "This is a lovely tree but it can struggle in urban conditions and is intolerant of drought." MoBot: "Hard to transplant because of its sparsely fibrous root system, and is best left undisturbed once planted in the landscape." RHS Cultivation: "Can be challenging to grow. Best grown in rich, moist, well-drained soils in full sun to part shade. Intolerant of root disturbance once established as well as drought". Heat/afternoon-shade guidance: NC State's Description: "Ideal growing conditions include full sun, with some afternoon shade the summer, and acidic soil that is moist and well-drained." MoBot Culture: "Perhaps best in full sun in northern climates, but appreciates some afternoon shade in hot summer climates." Disease/pathogen warnings: NC State's Insects, Diseases, or Other Plant Problems: "Sawflies do eat these trees. Do not plant where cotton has been grown as there is a pathogen that affects cotton that also affects Franklin trees." and "Wilt and root rot can also be serious problems. Consider planting in raised beds in areas with heavy clay." MoBot Problems: "Wilt and root rot can be serious problems. In general, this tree has a reputation for being difficult to grow." RHS's Diseases line independently corroborates the root-rot warning: 'Susceptible to Phytophthora root rot'.

is_houseplant is set to false by inference from NC State's outdoor USDA Hardiness Zone and Landscape Location framing (Container, Patio, Small space, all outdoor landscape/patio uses) and RHS/MoBot's outdoor cultivation prose; no admissible source frames this species as an indoor houseplant, but none explicitly states 'not a houseplant' either.

records.name_note: Sources split on how they present the common name. NC State's page title carries a six-name parenthetical (Kinnikinnik, Pale Dogwood, Red Willow, Silky Cornel, Silky Dogwood, Swamp Dogwood), and its Common Name(s) field stacks the same six in the same alphabetical order, so its first entry reflects alphabetization rather than a designated primary name. NC State's own Description prose opens 'Silky dogwood is a native, medium- to large-sized, deciduous shrub in the dogwood family.' MoBot's displayed Common Name field shows a single value, 'dogwood' -- the genus-level term also carried by sibling Cornus species already in this catalog, so it cannot serve as a species-distinguishing lead; MoBot's Noteworthy Characteristics prose instead calls the species 'silky dogwood' and adds that it 'is also commonly called swamp dogwood in reference to habitat and kinnkinnik (tobacco) in reference to a prior use of shrub bark by Native Americans as tobacco.' RHS's page for this binomial is titled 'Cornus amomum | silky dogwood', carries 'silky dogwood' as its plant-profile subtitle, and lists no other common names, so it is the only one of the three that designates a single lead common name and it breaks the tie. 'Silky Dogwood' is therefore used as common_name, with 'Swamp Dogwood' noted as a current alternate name carried in NC State's stacked list and in MoBot's prose.
unknowns: No admissible source among the ten authority domains carries a species-specific care page for Cornus amomum beyond NC State, MoBot, and RHS -- Clemson HGIC, UF/IFAS (edis.ifas.ufl.edu / ask.ifas.ufl.edu), Penn State Extension, University of Maryland Extension, and UGA fieldreport either have no dedicated page for this species or only mention it inside multi-species publications (rain-garden plant lists, dogwood pest factsheets), which per the rules cannot be used as species care sources for drainage, fertilizing, or watering schedules.

'Swamp Tupelo' is on NC State's list for this species but is not used as the lead because NC State's Nyssa biflora page lists Swamp Tupelo among that sibling species' common names. water_regime left null: no admissible source gives an explicit watering statement for this species. records.name_note: NC State's page title reads 'Ilex glabra (Appalachian Tea, Gallberry, Inkberry)' and its Common Name(s) list is alphabetized in that same order, so its first entry is Appalachian Tea. NC State's body prose nonetheless works in Inkberry: its Description opens 'Inkberry is a woody, multi-branched, broadleaf evergreen shrub in the holly family (Aquifoliaceae).' and its Uses (Ethnobotany) field calls Appalachian tea 'the sometimes used common name.' The lead name is taken from the two dedicated pages that designate a single primary: MoBot's Common Name field reads 'inkberry' and its Noteworthy Characteristics opens 'Ilex glabra, commonly called inkberry or gallberry'; RHS's page title is 'Ilex glabra | inkberry', with 'Appalachian tea tree, gallberry, ink berry, winterberry' listed separately under Other common names. 'Winterberry' is excluded as a lead candidate because NC State's dedicated Ilex verticillata page title is 'Ilex verticillata (Common Winterberry, Winterberry, Winterberry Holly)', assigning it to a sibling species already in this catalog.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State carries a human-scoped Poison block (no field or tag on the page scopes toxicity to cats or dogs specifically, and no "Poison Part" field is present on this page at all). Under "Poisonous to Humans": Poison Severity: "Low". Poison Symptoms: "Minor toxicity. Ingestion may cause vomiting, diarrhea, or other illness in humans." Poison Toxic Principle: "Saponins". Causes Contact Dermatitis: "No". A separate Edibility field states: "Use caution. Human ingestion of berries can cause minor toxic reaction." Missouri Botanical Garden's page carries no structured poison/toxicity field and does not state a toxicity scope; its prose does not address edibility; it says 'Gallberry honey is a highly-rated honey that results from bees feeding on inkberry flowers.' No admissible source scopes any toxicity statement to cats or dogs specifically, so toxic_to_pets is left null per the cat/dog-scoping rule; see unknowns. RHS's Potentially harmful field reads: 'Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling. Pets: Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten - see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants for further information and useful contact numbers' -- a handling warning and an unscoped Pets line that names no animal. The sources disagree on edibility: the same NC State page that cautions against human ingestion tags the fruit Edible in its Fruit Value To Gardener field, 'Edible fruit' under Play Value and '#edible fruits' in its Tags list, while RHS says the fruit is not to be eaten.
unknowns: scientific_name_accepted was set at landing to Ilex glabra on RHS's dedicated page (rhs.org.uk/plants/20984/ilex-glabra/details, H1 'Ilex glabra', title 'Ilex glabra | inkberry', Name Status 'Correct'), which the audit reached after the researcher's searches surfaced only Ilex aquifolium results and cultivar pages; its title, Other common names and Potentially harmful fields are cited at landing.

toxic_to_pets: NC State's Poison block is scoped only to humans ('Poisonous to Humans', symptoms state '...in humans') with no Problem-for-Cats/Problem-for-Dogs tags found anywhere on the page, and no other admissible source (MoBot) states a toxicity scope at all, so toxic_to_pets is left null rather than inferred from the human-scoped data.

soil_ph: NC State's structured Soil pH field reads 'Acid (<6.0)', which is an open-ended band per the schema rules (no floor or ceiling may be read off it), and no RHS pH field was available to check against in either direction (see scientific_name_accepted note on RHS being unavailable for this species), so soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are both left null.

soil_drainage: NC State's own structured Soil Drainage field reads 'Good Drainage, Moist, Occasionally Wet' which maps to moderate per the schema rules; this is cited first and preferred over MoBot's Culture prose ('Tolerates wet soils. Prefers rich, consistently moist, acidic soils') and MoBot's structured 'Water: Medium to wet' field, both of which lean wetter and are treated as disclosed counterpoints rather than the basis for moisture_retentive.

water_regime: MoBot's structured field reads 'Water: Medium to wet', which does not cleanly match any of the four enum tokens (it exceeds a bare 'Medium' but is not a directive to keep soil constantly moist/boggy), and no species-specific watering-instruction sentence was found on either admissible page, so water_regime is left null rather than guessed.

direct_sun_hours_max: NC State's Light field gives hour ranges (6+ hours for Full Sun, 2-6 hours for Partial Shade) but these are the site-wide legend definitions for those light categories, not species-specific prose about how much direct sun this particular plant tolerates or needs, so per the schema rules this field is left null.

fertilize fields and day/night/humidity/light_fc fields: no admissible source (NC State, MoBot) gave any fertilizing schedule, temperature range, humidity requirement, or foot-candle light measurement for this in-ground landscape shrub, so all these fields are left null.

is_houseplant is set to false based on both sources describing Ilex glabra exclusively as an outdoor, USDA-hardiness-zoned (NC State: zones 4a-11b; MoBot: zones 4-9) landscape/garden shrub used for hedges, screens, and naturalized plantings, with no houseplant use mentioned by either source.

Fire risk: NC State's page carries an explicit high-flammability warning, reproduced verbatim in the fire_risk citation below, and its cultivar list separately flags 'Compacta' as high flammability; the species-level Fire Risk Rating field itself (independent of any cultivar) also reads 'high flammability.'

normalizations: 2026-09-05: fifty-second batch (cruise throttle) -- native trees and shrubs: Cucumber Tree, Bottlebrush Buckeye, Franklin Tree, Silky Dogwood, Water Tupelo, and Inkberry. Clean first run (12/12 agents, 1.37M subagent tokens); land_check.py and covered.py clean; verify_quotes.py 89/91 reachable quotes before repair, both MISSes fixed here (a Plant Type quote that dropped the 'Poisonous' entry -- a trimmed safety trait -- and NC State Light strings paraphrased with rewritten parentheticals). One value changed: Water Tupelo's soil_ph_min 6.0, a floor the record had read off the absence of NC State's Acid checkbox, was nulled because RHS's pH field reads 'Acid or Neutral' and both NC State's and MoBot's prose say the species prefers acidic soils. Two accepted names were restored with values unchanged (Franklin Tree's one-word 'Correct' quote paired with the title and NC State's Previously known as list; Inkberry's on RHS's page 20984, which the researcher had reported not found and the auditor reached -- H1, title, Name Status, Other common names and Potentially harmful field all cited).
